articles.title: 5 public universities in Illinois use controversial Flock cameras to surveil campus, records show
articles.description:
As towns, cities and colleges in Illinois and across the country cut ties with Flock Safety, a comprehensive review of contracts by WBEZ found that five of the state’s 12 public universities still work with the controversial surveillance technology company.

That includes the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the largest campus in the state, and the University of Illinois Chicago, which is in the process of renewing its contract. Southern Illinois University Carbondale even employs a Flock surveillance drone that costs more than $40,000 a year.

These schools, in addition to Western Illinois University and the University of Illinois Springfield, have spent more than $450,000 on Flock’s services since 2021, records show.

Flock’s automatic license plate readers use cameras and artificial intelligence to capture data about every passing vehicle, including plate numbers, make and model and even dents and bumper stickers. That information is uploaded to a database that can be searched by campus police, as well as outside law enforcement agencies, to see where a vehicle and its driver have been and when.

College leaders say the surveillance helps solve crimes and keep campuses and students safe.

But Flock has come under intense public scrutiny following revelations that police officers have used the company’s surveillance cameras to stalk their exes. Data captured by Flock cameras have also led to wrongful arrests. At universities like UIC and Western Illinois University, students have started petitions calling on administrators to end their relationships with the company.

Some students and faculty say the use of Flock equipment to surveil American campuses is especially troubling because universities are meant to be places where people can discuss and study ideas freely. They worry Flock cameras could be used to identify and discipline students and faculty if they attend a protest or express opinions universities and the federal government find problematic.

People worry “they will be singled out, they could face repercussions, and all of that is really, in my mind, antithetical to the ideals of the university,” said Torin Monahan, a surveillance researcher at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.

The presence of Flock cameras adds another layer of concern at schools like UIC that pride themselves on supporting underrepresented and marginalized students, because the data collected can endanger immigrant and international students and students of color.

Last year, an audit by the Illinois secretary of state found that U.S. Customs and Border Protection had searched Flock databases across Illinois in violation of the state’s Trust Act, which bans cooperation between Illinois law enforcement and federal immigration authorities. Earlier in 2025, the same state office found that Texas agents searched Flock databases in Illinois to pursue a woman who had an abortion.

Flock claims the company has made changes in the last year that allow police forces to limit who can access camera data. But as of this summer, outside agencies were still frequently searching the data collected at some Illinois public colleges.

In early August, WBEZ filed a public records request for a log of external agencies that had searched Flock data from the University of Illinois System since early 2025 and for what reasons.

System officials said the request was too burdensome because it turned up such a large volume of data — and revealed that outside law enforcement had searched Flock data from the three campuses more than 650,000 times over a 30-day period in July and August.

“The police I've been interviewing will say that they want to protect the campus community,” Monahan said.

But he questioned if university administrators want to be embracing this “fortress mentality” given the many trade-offs. “Do they want to be on the wrong side of these privacy concerns and these surveillance risks to their populations?”

‘Why are we gathering this giant pool of information?’

Among Illinois public universities, the University of Illinois System is Flock’s biggest client.

UIC has a two-year, $110,300 contract with Flock to operate 15 cameras on university property, according to documents obtained through public records requests.

UIC leaders denied a request for an interview. But spokesperson Sherri McGinnis Gonzalez said via email that Flock’s surveillance technology enables “investigators to identify vehicles associated with reported crimes, public safety threats and Amber Alerts.”

She said the university’s contract ends this month, but officials are in talks to renew it.

“The safety of our students, faculty, staff, patients and visitors is a top priority,” McGinnis Gonzalez wrote. “UIC is committed to transparency, accountability and privacy protections in its use of public safety technology.”

In addition to its contract with Flock, UIC officials agreed in December 2025 to pay a company called Volt Inc. $3.5 million over three years for AI-powered video detection of weapons, “crowd formation” and “unattended objects,” public records show.

A university spokesperson said via email that campus police hired Volt “to detect potential security issues in real time and quickly alert UIC Police, helping improve campus safety,” adding that the Flock and Volt systems operate separately.

Flock signed the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as its first public university client in the state in 2021, records show. A university spokesperson said the campus has since paid more than $180,000 to the company.

Leaders there denied an interview request. But in a written statement, a spokesperson said their Flock surveillance network of 20 cameras had “recently proved integral in investigations involving sexual assault, robbery, suicidal or missing persons, aggravated battery, and stolen vehicles, just to name a few.”

SIU Carbondale officials denied a request for an interview and refused to answer questions over email.

In all, more than 150,000 students at Illinois public universities are subject to surveillance on their campuses by Flock’s AI-powered tech, whether they are driving to class or getting dropped off in their family car on move-in day. That's in addition to the many faculty, visitors and others who drive by campus daily.

Monahan said he worries not only about student privacy, but also about data security. Flock claims that local agencies own the data from their cameras, but that data is housed on Flock-owned servers, Monahan said, and used to train Flock’s AI models.

“What are you learning about the people on a campus through these systems that can then be fed into these artificial intelligence systems and monetized by a third party, such as Flock?” Monahan asked.

Some students have similar concerns.

“Why are we gathering this giant pool of information just in case it might help if somebody's car might get stolen and drive on this road?” said Ellie Prafcke, a visiting student at UIC. “I feel like there are many other ways that we can solve crimes rather than just taking in random data.”

Prafcke and her friend Rachel Stein said they hope UIC leaders will take the time to get feedback from students before they sign off on a new contract with Flock. The two even have an idea for how to go about doing so.

“Set up a sign right here,” Stein said, pointing to a camera in front of UIC’s computer design building. Tell students: “This is a Flock camera. This is what it does. Here's a QR code to tell us your opinion about whether you want this here or not.”

“Then before you sign the contract,” Stein said, “think about what the students want.”

Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with Open Campus.

Related
  • What to know about Flock’s controversial license plate readers
  • Flock license plate readers turn Chicago suburbs into ground zero for bitter fight over surveillance
  • Illinois suburbs halt Flock use, suspend officers and review policy amid alleged improper use

articles.title: Alsip Mayor John Ryan helped establish term limits in his town. Now that they affect him, will they be eased?
articles.description:
A decade ago while a trustee on the Alsip village board, John Ryan led the charge to impose term limits on the mayor and other elected officials in the south suburb so nobody would be able to serve more than three consecutive four-year terms.

He marshaled enough support on the village board to get a binding referendum placed on the 2016 ballot, letting Alsip voters decide whether to impose those limits, which they did.

Today, Ryan is Alsip’s mayor and in the midst of his third consecutive term — but it may not be his last, after all.

That’s because his colleagues on the village board — with what the village clerk says was Ryan's support — recently decided to place a new referendum on the ballot in November that, if passed by Alsip voters, would extend term limits to four consecutive four-year terms.

That would provide an obvious benefit for Ryan should the ballot question pass, and should he run again and win. He’d not only stay in power longer, he would continue to get paid by taxpayers and accrue more service credits that would boost his public sector pension.

Among those to find an irony in the situation is Patrick Kitching, who was Alsip’s mayor at the time Ryan pushed for the 2016 referendum.

Calling his successor "no good," Kitching described this as another opportunistic policy reversal by Ryan, like when he pushed for a cut in the mayor’s salary while Kitching was in office and later, when Ryan took over, wanted a mayoral pay hike.

A bitter political rival of Ryan, Kitching fought the initial term limit, arguing he was a full-time mayor and while limits at the federal and state levels make sense, they could prohibit someone at the local level from growing into and becoming better at the job.

“Show me a town that has a full-time mayor and has term limits,” he said then, according to a Daily Southtown article. “Three terms for a mayor is ridiculous. We are all subject to term limits — it’s called voting.”

But Ryan argued at the time, according to the news story: “The mayor made every attempt to obstruct voters’ rights. Just let the voters decide.”

The village board approved that ballot question, Kitching vetoed it and the village board then overrode the veto.

Of the 4,716 people who ended up voting on the 2016 referendum, 3,832 supported the limits, or more than 80%, according to election records.

Read Alsip’s new resolution, ballot question

In August, the Alsip village board approved a resolution to place the question about changing the term limits on the Nov. 3 ballot.

The resolution includes wording similar to Kitching’s long-ago argument, saying “the Mayor and Board of Trustees recognize that maintaining experienced leadership while continuously encouraging qualified public service ensures efficient and stable municipal management.”

Asked about the new effort, Ryan told the Chicago Sun-Times via email: “We are not trying to undo term limits. The Alsip Village Board approved a resolution to place a question on the November 3, 2026, ballot, asking Alsip voters whether they wish to modify the consecutive term limits for the mayor, clerk and trustees from three terms to four.”

Ryan didn’t respond to further questions, including his feelings on the proposed change to the term limits. He didn’t have to vote on the matter at the August meeting, but he registered no objection and publicly said it needed to be approved that night to meet the deadline for the ballot.

He won’t say whether he plans to run for reelection as his current term expires in 2029.

The existing term limits, when approved in 2016, were not applied retroactively, so even though Kitching was in the midst of his third term at the time, the restrictions went in place after the 2017 election. That means he would’ve been allowed to serve out three more consecutive terms if he won the corresponding elections.

But Kitching opted not to run again.

Instead, Ryan ran for mayor in 2017 and won by 60 votes against another opponent.

Ryan has been mayor of the community of just under 20,000 people ever since, most recently winning in the 2025 election while running unopposed.

Alsip Village Clerk Renee Harding says of the new term limit measure: “If this passes” as a referendum, Ryan “would be allowed to run for one more term” of four years, “not an additional 3 terms.”

Harding says Ryan “supports putting it on the ballot and hopes it passes so he can run for another term."

Other suburbs with term limits include Tinley Park and Skokie.

Related

articles.title: 'Starved Rock killer' died last year, but his family is now seeking a rare posthumous pardon from Pritzker
articles.description:
The decades-long fight to clear Chester Weger’s name as the notorious "Starved Rock Killer" isn’t ending with his death.

Weger’s family will get a chance next month to argue that the man who spent nearly six decades behind bars was wrongly convicted in one of Illinois’ most infamous murder cases.

The Illinois Prisoner Review Board has scheduled a rare Oct. 6 hearing in Chicago on the family’s request for a posthumous pardon from Gov. JB Pritzker.

The board rarely has considered posthumous clemency petitions, holding such hearings for only two other people in the past seven years.

Weger was sentenced to life in prison in 1961 for killing one of the three women whose battered bodies were found near a cave at Starved Rock State Park, a popular getaway spot for Chicagoans.

He confessed to the killings but quickly recanted — then spent the rest of his life insisting he was innocent.

Weger was paroled in 2020 for good behavior in prison after spending about 60 years behind bars, but his conviction remained on his record.

After his release, his lawyers launched a fresh effort to overturn the conviction, citing DNA evidence, new witness testimony and alternative theories about who killed Mildred Linquist, 50, Lillian Oetting, 50, and Frances Murphy, 47. They had gone to Starved Rock to hike and bird watch in March 1960.

Weger's lawyers have theorized that a relative of one victim hired mobsters to kill her and that the other two women were slain because they witnessed the crime.

The lawyers also pointed to a hair found on the finger of one of the victims. Tests found the hair didn't match the women or Weger and most likely came from another local man.

But a LaSalle County judge rejected Weger’s post-conviction petition last year. Weger died less than a week later. He was 86.

His family filed a petition in June asking Pritzker to grant executive clemency — a process separate from parole and one that could posthumously wipe away Weger's conviction.

The Prisoner Review Board will weigh the testimony given Oct. 6 before sending the governor a confidential recommendation. Pritzker will make the final call.

The board typically takes about two months to forward its recommendation. Another high-profile clemency request — from former Gangster Disciples boss Larry Hoover — remains pending after an April hearing.

“We didn't get a fair shot at the evidentiary hearing,” says Weger attorney Andrew Hale, who spent a decade reinvestigating the Starved Rock murders, hosted a podcast about the killings and appeared in an HBO documentary about them.

Hale says Weger's sister and her two daughters plan to attend the October hearing. He hopes the board members will closely review the family's nearly 100-page clemency petition.

"I am hopeful," he says. "I feel like this board and the governor's office, if they take a fresh look at this, I should win."

He acknowledges that wiping away Weger's conviction could potentially open the door to a lawsuit, but says that's not the family's focus.

Prosecutors and survivors of the women have opposed the efforts to parole Weger and overturn his conviction.

One of the few recent cases in Illinois in which a posthumous clemency hearing was held involved Grover Thompson, who was convicted of attempted murder after a trial in 1981.

Thompson was convicted of stabbing a 71-year-old woman during an attempted sexual assault in her Mount Vernon apartment. He died in prison in 1996.

Years later, serial killer Timothy Krajcir confessed to an attempted sexual assault matching the circumstances of the crime for which Thompson had been convicted.

Krajcir admitted to killing nine women and is serving an 80-year Illinois prison sentence.

Thompson’s nephew, the Illinois Innocence Project and police officer Paul Echols — who obtained Krajcir’s confession — pushed to clear Thompson’s name.

Then-Gov. Bruce Rauner granted Thompson a pardon in 2019.

The other recent case involves Joe James, a Black man executed in 1908 for killing a white man, Clergy Ballard, in Springfield.

Northwestern University’s Center on Wrongful Convictions and other advocates have argued James did not receive a fair trial.

An all-white jury convicted him just weeks after a white mob lynched two Black men and torched hundreds of Black homes and businesses during the Springfield race riot.

The Prisoner Review Board has sent Pritzker a confidential recommendation in James' case, and the governor has yet to act on it, according to a board spokesperson.

articles.title: In Little Village, a year after Midway Blitz, some vow to stay, others worry they can't afford to
articles.description:
Little Village faced displacement and gentrification pressures long before Operation Midway Blitz. It’s part of South Lawndale, where in 2024, nearly half of renters were spending more than 30% of their income on housing. The neighborhood’s proximity to downtown and rapidly gentrifying Pilsen–Little Village's boundaries are roughly from Cermak to 31st Street, and from Sacramento to Kostner–had also fueled concerns that development could push longtime residents and businesses out.

The COVID-19 pandemic brought another period of upheaval, forcing some businesses to close and leaving others struggling.

Then came President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

During the height of Operation Midway Blitz, federal immigration agents detained 3,841 people, according to federal data analyzed by the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ.

Little Village became one of the most visible targets. Federal agents made arrests in the neighborhood on the first full day of Midway Blitz and returned repeatedly in the months that followed.

On Oct. 22 and 23 and again on Nov. 8, large groups of federal agents descended on Little Village, carrying out arrests and confronting residents and protesters. The Illinois Accountability Commission later singled out those three days for an investigation of what it described as an “occupation” of the neighborhood.

The effects extended beyond the arrests. Fear of immigration agents kept people home. Shops and restaurants emptied, battering Little Village’s commercial corridors. A University of Illinois Chicago analysis released this month estimated that increased immigration enforcement that started in January of 2025 resulted in $1.26 billion in lost retail and restaurant activity across Cook County over the course of the following year. Researchers said residents of neighborhoods with large numbers of “Latin America-born” people made fewer trips to stores and restaurants outside their communities, a dip that continued for nearly a year.

Immigration enforcement is quieter and less visible now, but the Trump administration continues to arrest hundreds of people each month.

In Little Village, many continue to stay home, and some business owners are spending money accumulated over generations to remain open. Some are questioning whether they can afford to stay there.

The Sun-Times spoke with residents, business owners and a neighborhood realtor about how immigration enforcement is reshaping Little Village—straining businesses, prompting property offers and leading some residents to invest in Mexico as they reconsider their futures in Chicago.

She fought displacement. Now she is wondering whether she can stay

María de la Luz Rodríguez, 61, who’s lived in Little Village for 19 years, started working with the housing cooperative Cooperativa La Villita after watching apartment buildings change hands and tenants get pushed out. Rodríguez, from Veracruz, Mexico, helped develop and write the cooperative’s bylaws in Spanish and English, handed out flyers and spoke at community meetings. Eventually, the cooperative purchased its first building, a six-unit property on Whipple Street. According to its website, estimated monthly housing charges range from $950 to $1,150. By this summer, Rodríguez says, all of its apartments were occupied and the group was working toward buying another.

“The cooperative is a group of people who really love Little Village,” Rodríguez says in Spanish.

But Rodríguez, who does not have legal status, says her own ability to remain in Little Village has become uncertain. She lost her retail job after her employer began using the federal system E-Verify to check whether staffers are authorized to work in the United States.

She planned to purchase a cooperative membership but could not afford to after she became unemployed. She continues to volunteer as a board member.

She also lost work as a community health promoter after funding dried up. Now she is struggling to cover her rent.

Peddling has become one way to get by. The Street Vendors Association of Chicago gave her $500 in assistance. She packs buñuelos and Veracruz-style peanuts into a suitcase and takes her wares to community and health fairs because there is more foot traffic than the Little Village business corridor.

“Little Village is dead,” she says.

Rodríguez says people in Little Village do not want to leave. Neighbors watch out for one another.

She is nevertheless considering leaving herself.

Rodríguez has family in Mexico and is thinking about returning to Veracruz. “There may not be much money there,” she says, “But at least I can have a coffee outside in my garden, or go outside for a walk and they are not going to grab me.”

A home somewhere else

Erika Villegas, 44, has worked with homeowners in Little Village for years. The RE/MAX broker says families there tend to hold onto their properties for decades, resulting in relatively little turnover.

But Villegas is seeing some immigrant families consider a different future.

Villegas says she has worked with several Little Village clients who have invested in property in Mexico, including families who are looking for a possible place to live in the future. The developers she works with are primarily in larger Mexican cities, while she believes Little Village families who actually return to Mexico may be more likely to go back to their hometowns.

There are other signs that more Chicago-area families are keeping Mexico within reach. Requests at the Mexican Consulate in Chicago to register U.S.-born people for Mexican nationality more than doubled, from 3,800 in 2024 to 9,646 in 2025, according to the consulate.

Through Villegas’ network, land can start at about $35,000, condos at $100,000 and homes at $135,000.

“You don’t know what the future looks like because of the current policy, and what it will continue to do to families long term,” she says.

Villegas has built a network of contacts in Mexico who can help clients find housing, start businesses and make a living. For families considering leaving the United States, she says, her job is not simply to sell their home but to help them figure out what comes next.

“What is the plan,” she says, “and how can we get you to that plan?”

Villegas says someone who has paid off a home over decades may be able to buy a house for substantially less in parts of Mexico and live on what remains.

But she has encountered homeowners prepared to accept unsolicited offers before realizing they could be giving up $50,000, $60,000 or $70,000 in equity.

The decision to buy in Mexico is rarely about one thing, she says. An owner may be dealing with problems involving tenants, building repair costs or a business that is struggling. Immigration status can make navigating those problems even harder.

Eventually, Villegas says, the pressures can accumulate.

“Sometimes people just are also tired,” she says. “Sometimes people don’t have the will to fight anymore.”

Going where the customers are

Around 1 p.m. on Aug. 13, Los Candiles restaurant at 2624 S. Central Ave. was nearly empty.

José Luis (Louie) López was there with a kitchen worker and his wife, Clarita López, 40, who waits tables. There were plenty of tables but few customers.

López, 44, pulled out the paper calendars he keeps to record the number of kitchen orders the restaurant fills each day. Before the pandemic, the restaurant typically recorded 40 to 50 kitchen orders on weekdays. Saturdays could bring as many as 90. Sundays, helped by church traffic, could reach 110.

He pointed to this year’s calendar. One Tuesday had 12 orders. Another day had 14. Saturdays that once reached 90 were now in the 30s.

“Everything is at half,” López says.

His parents opened Los Candiles in 1995. The family owns the building and finished paying it off about a decade ago. That has spared López a rent or mortgage payment as business has fallen.

But owning the building has not brought customers through the door.

López says immigration enforcement is only part of what has hurt the restaurant. Food costs have risen and customers have less money to spend. When rumors spread that immigration agents have returned, he says, people become frightened again.

To cope, he has increasingly taken Los Candiles outside Little Village.

López began offering taquizas, or catered taco parties, in 2017. He brings a flat-top grill, rice and beans, tortillas and trays of toppings and cooks for customers on site.

“That’s what’s keeping our head above water,” Lopez says.

He approached Cody’s Public House, a bar in Lakeview with an idea for selling tacos there on Thursdays. The relationship eventually became a weekly gig.

López says Los Candiles can sell more tacos during four hours at Cody’s than during seven hours at the restaurant in Little Village.

“We made double the tips.”

Without catering and the taquizas, López says, “We would have been long gone.”

The offers are coming

Baltazar Enriquez, 46, never stops moving. The president of the Little Village Community Council zips from one conversation to another with the people seeking advice and help at his office. School supplies and diapers are on hand for people in need. When immigration agents began operating heavily in Little Village last fall, he became one of the neighborhood’s most visible organizers, warning residents about reported ICE sightings and helping coordinate community response. He also owns a five-unit building in the 2300 block of South Trumbull Ave.

Unsolicited real estate inquiries about his property are not new. Enriquez says they began picking up during the COVID-19 pandemic. But since Midway Blitz’s last fall they have become much more frequent.

“I get mail, phone calls, emails,” Enriquez says. On some days, Enriquez estimates he receives as many as 30 solicitations. Some ask whether he wants to sell. Others offer financing. He has saved screenshots of text messages from people asking about his property, as well as a late-August mailer from Sherman Property, a cash home-buying business, designed to look like a check made out to him for $316,222.

He says prospective buyers have offered as much as $1 million to purchase his building. He has refused.

One of his tenants, a senior who has lived in the building for 15 years, still pays $800 a month for a three-bedroom apartment. Enriquez says the man has told him that if the rent went up, he would have to leave and start over somewhere else, away from the doctors and neighborhood he knows. He says a new owner could charge $1,300 or $1,500 for the same unit.

Little Village businesses are still recovering from months when customers stayed home amid immigration enforcement. Property owners are dealing with higher taxes and the costs of maintaining aging buildings.The ICE operations, he believes, made things worse.

“They put [in] more fuel,” he says.

Enriquez has spent years trying to build a life, investments and a future in Little Village. The question, he says, is whether everyone else will have the same choice.

The cost of staying

Around 4 p.m. on Aug. 13 Osito’s Tap was quiet and dimly lit. A bartender arranged liquor bottles as Mike Moreno Jr., 35, settled into a table nearby. The first customers had yet to arrive.

Moreno’s family has been doing business in Little Village for more than half a century. His grandfather operated grocery stores in the neighborhood and his father opened Moreno’s Liquors on 26th Street in 1977. Moreno later opened Osito’s Tap near 26th and Ridgeway.

The family has survived difficult times before, including the COVID-19 pandemic. But Moreno says immigration enforcement operations brought another kind of strain.

From August through November last year, business at Osito’s and Moreno’s Liquors fell by half for two months and by at least 25% during the other two, Moreno says. The family cut costs and expanded delivery. They avoided layoffs.

They also began spending savings.

“We’re literally taking it from generations and generations, years and years of wealth that we built, and just reinvesting it and popping it back into our own businesses,” Moreno says.

Moreno’s family owns properties in Little Village and has no intention of selling. But he says the inquiries from speculators have become increasingly difficult to ignore.

Before the ICE arrests, Moreno says, he might receive four or five calls a week from people interested in buying property or offering financing. Now, he sometimes gets four or five in a day.

Moreno says one caller told him he had seen media reports about the raids and their economic impact on Little Village businesses before asking about Moreno’s property.

He usually blocks the numbers.

“We’re not selling,” Moreno says. “We’ve been here for almost 50 years, and we’ll be here for another 50.”

“As long as we work really hard,” Moreno says, “we can keep what’s ours.”

articles.title: A law requires Illinois schools to teach Asian American history. Is it happening?
articles.description:
In 2021, Illinois passed a law requiring every public elementary and high school to teach a unit of Asian American and Pacific Islander history.

Five years later, many schools throughout the state have yet to fully implement the Teaching Equitable Asian American Community History Act.

The Illinois State Board of Education developed a resource guide to help schools build out AAPI history curricula. State Rep. Jennifer Gong-Gershowitz, D-Glenview, says she’s proud of the progress that’s been made so far — but there’s still work to be done.

Some advocates say they were met with mixed results while doing outreach to schools.

“Roughly 25% of teachers and students in the state of Illinois have had some participation with the Asian American curricular resources that have been made available since the bill passed,” Gong-Gershowitz, a sponsor of the bill, told WBEZ.

In 2026, WBEZ talked to Chicago-area educators, students and lawmakers about the TEAACH Act to see how the law has taken shape in some local schools.

What led to the TEAACH Act?

Gong-Gershowitz said the momentum for the bill was prompted largely by high-profile cases of anti-Asian hate crimes during the COVID-19 pandemic. She presented the bill in committee the day after a mass shooting in March at several Atlanta-area spas killed eight people, including six Asian women.

A coalition of more than 35 organizations, including Asian Americans Advancing Justice Chicago, championed the bill — the first of its kind anywhere in the United States.

Some of the bill’s opponents said decisions about curricula should happen at the local level, rather than being mandated by the state.

The bill ultimately passed the Illinois State House 108-10 on May 31, 2021. A committee of local educators worked together to organize resources and standardize a curriculum.

The TEAACH Act was unfunded when it first passed, but in 2025, Illinois committed $2 million to inclusive K-12 history mandates. Some of that money was allocated to meeting the TEAACH Act’s mandate. But a standardized statewide Asian American history curriculum still hasn’t been established.

Why is it important to teach AAPI history?

Education researchers have found that students who participate in ethnic studies are more academically engaged, develop a stronger sense of personal empowerment, perform better academically and graduate at higher rates.

A WBEZ analysis of census data showed the Asian population in metro Chicago grew by an estimated 11.6% since 2020, more than double the rate of growth for the next highest group. Roughly 9.4 million people lived in the Chicago metropolitan statistical area in 2024, and around 764,000 identified themselves as Asian — almost 80,000 more than in 2020.

Laura Ouk, board president of the National Cambodian Heritage Museum and Killing Fields Memorial in Chicago, wants more teachers to get on board with the TEAACH Act because she’s seen the impact of education on young people.

“Something that I think a lot of Asian American/Pacific Islanders can identify with: We weren’t always proud of who we are, and I think a lot of it was because we didn’t really know who we were,” Ouk, who has been an educator for 14 years, said. “Now, the younger generations are just so proud of who they are, so that they [don’t] have to repeat that cycle of not knowing how that impacts them later on in life.”

What are schools doing to teach AAPI history now?

The Albany Park-based immigration rights nonprofit HANA Center surveyed 113 students, teachers and parents about the TEAACH Act in fall 2023. It found 73% of student respondents say they received “little to no” education focusing on Asian American communities during the previous school year.

Some educators have seen those percentages play out in the classroom.

John Lee teaches an Asian American Studies elective at Niles West High School in Skokie. He estimates he instructs up to about 13% of the senior class.

Lee says about half of his students haven’t heard about fundamental moments from Asian American history in his curriculum before starting his class. It includes historical events like the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965. Niles West didn’t respond to Lee’s comments when asked. Instead, the school shared a description for its semester-long Asian American History course.

The Illinois State Board of Education said in a statement that individual school districts determine how schools meet the requirements of the TEAACH Act within their local curriculum.

What are Illinois schools doing about the TEAACH Act mandate?

WBEZ checked in with several Chicago-area schools to get a sense of how they’re implementing the mandate.

In a statement, Chicago Public Schools told WBEZ: "The District’s Social Science Department actively curates lessons and offers content and pedagogical resources for K-12 teachers. These materials align with the IL Mandated Units of Study, including the TEAACH Act, and support the development of more inclusive Social Science classrooms, where all units of study are explored from multiple perspectives."

Township High School District 214, which covers multiple suburbs north of Chicago, said in a statement that its U.S. history curriculum provides “opportunities to explore the contributions of Asian Americans throughout U.S. history”.

“When the TEAACH Act was first introduced, I think over the course of the five years we've made meaningful progress,” said Bradford Hubbard, the district’s Associate Superintendent for Teaching and Learning. “I also think at the same time we can certainly do better.”

Hubbard said he’s working to create a new process that would help administrators evaluate whether the course is fulfilling the state’s mandated units of study, including Asian American history.

Related
  • Illinois schools have been required to teach Asian American history for 5 years. How is it going?

That change could be a slow, multiyear process, Hubbard added. The district is considering bigger changes to their larger social sciences department.

“Does the current graduation requirement need to be evaluated? Are we able to fit everything in that we feel like we need to, but then we're also mandated to, into what we currently offer?” Hubbard said.

Laura Ouk does outreach to school administrators to introduce them to Asian American history resources. She said in the years since the TEAACH Act passed, some schools still aren’t making the material a priority.

“Sometimes, it’s as indirect as just not responding to our emails and our calls,” Ouk said. “And then sometimes, it is more direct, where we are in meetings and hearing them just not want to prioritize it, because maybe it’s a combination of time and not having enough teachers who are teaching a certain class.”

Resources for teachers who want to learn how to teach Asian American history are already being offered. They include free workshops and online training from the University of Illinois that allows teachers to work toward an ISBE microcredential in Asian American history. The nonprofit Asian Americans Advancing Justice Chicago said it organized 63 professional development workshops related to the TEAACH Act from July 2022 to June 2023.

Have other states passed laws similar to the TEAACH Act?

Some states have established AAPI requirements through a patchwork of different laws and standards.

A California law signed in 2021 requires all high schools in the state to offer an ethnic studies course. The class will be a statewide graduation requirement beginning in 2030.

In 2022, New Jersey became the second state after Illinois to require schools to teach Asian American and Pacific Islander history. The act went into effect the 2022–2023 school year. The mandate was also unfunded when it passed.

What do students say about Asian American history courses?

In April, members of the HANA Center’s Suburban Youth Council spoke at Chicago-area board of education meetings in several school districts. The group is pushing the districts to fully implement the TEAACH Act. That includes ensuring accomplishments by Asian American people are included in history curricula and including at least two pieces of Asian American literature in English courses.

Ahir Naveen, a junior at John Hersey High School in Arlington Heights, is working to collect student signatures in support of their demands and return to leadership with the petition.

“I think that with knowledge comes power, and with knowledge comes understanding of other people and perspectives broadening,” Naveen said.

articles.title: Scott Jennings humiliated as CNN panel laughs at his 'comedic' Trump hypothetical
articles.description: Conservative CNN pundit Scott Jennings botched an attempt to defend President Donald Trump's tariffs with a hypothetical that led to everyone laughing in his face. On Wednesday, Jennings was part of the roundtable on CNN Newsnight, and he tried to back up Trump's handling of the economy by posing a question to the other pundits, including former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio , New York Times reporter Lulu Garcia-Navarro and Democratic political strategist Bakari Sellers. "I have a sincere question for you because you all very concerned about the tariffs as taxes," Jennings said, referring to critics' argument that tariffs function as a tax on American consumers because importers pass the cost along as higher prices. "If Donald Trump tomorrow said, 'I'll trade you elimination of all tariffs for elimination of all corporate income taxes,' would you take the deal?" The panel responded with faces of confusion. De Blasio squinted his eyes and turned his head sideways while Garcia-Navarro threw her hands up and stared blankly at Jennings. No one responded for several seconds until host Abby Phillip asked, "What is that, Scott?" "Would you take all taxes down to zero?" Jennings asked. De Blasio, still squinting, shook his head and said, "No," while Garcia-Navarro waved the question away. "What is the point of that hypothetical, Scott?" Phillip asked. As Jennings took himself seriously, everyone else at the table began cracking up as he tried to explain, "The point is this, because you're mad about certain taxes, but every Democrat constantly argues for tax increases on corporations against tariffs. It makes no sense." "Scott, you're the conservative at this table. That's why this is so comedic," Phillip explained while Jennings, with an angry expression, turned to Sellers, who was laughing with the other pundits still, and yelled, "Do you not understand this? It's a very simple argument!" "You have to bend over backwards to explain the conservative rationale for tariffs, and I don't see you doing it," Phillip said. "You keep telling me this is what Trump believes."

articles.title: U.S. Postal Service Chief Is Reportedly So Fed Up He Wants to Quit
articles.description: Postmaster General David Steiner wants out. The United States Postal Service chief told individuals close to him that he wants to resign from his post, according to a report from Reuters on Wednesday. “The message was, this isn’t what he signed up for, and he didn’t come on board to get beat up like this,” one source said. This report comes as President Trump has been attempting to use the supposedly independent mail service to do his bidding in his last-minute midterm election interference, commanding it to only deliver ballots if they had a unique barcode and if states handed over voter lists to the agency. The Supreme Court struck that dream down on Monday, just two days before reports of Steiner’s discontent. USPS has denied the report, saying it has “absolutely zero ⁠validity.” Steiner was apparently most discouraged after an intense Senate hearing earlier this summer in which he essentially admitted under oath that USPS would bend the knee to Trump’s attacks on vote-by-mail. Sen. Peters: "Yes or no, if a state refuses to turn their absentee voter list over to the federal government, will the Postal Service still mail their ballots under this proposed rule?" Postmaster General David Steiner: "Under our proposed regulation, no." pic.twitter.com/4JYe7Jo450 — The Bulwark (@BulwarkOnline) June 24, 2026 However, sources familiar with Steiner’s plans told Reuters his discontent stretched back even further. The White House was making efforts to assuage Steiner since the end of last year, with donors even setting him up on a golf outing with Trump on one of his properties in Florida in December.

articles.title: 'Cannot go on!' Trump melts down after Federal Reserve defies his wishes
articles.description: President Donald Trump took to his Truth Social platform on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve agreed to a significant increase in interest rates — demanding that they do the opposite and make a massive cut instead. "Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR," wrote Trump. "Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment! If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year." "The word 'Deficit' is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS," Trump continued. "We are 'carrying' almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" Economists broadly agree that while reductions in interest rates make borrowing cheaper and boost employment in the short run, it can also drive a run of high inflation even higher. Increases to interest rates are one of the Fed's primary tools to tamp down inflation, which has been surging due to fuel shortages from the war in Iran. Trump has put intense pressure on the Fed, an independent body intended not to be influenced by political considerations, to cut interest rates to time a surge of economic activity when Republicans need a boost in the midterm elections.
